idiom_name: explicit (void) cast on a discarded result, with an errno note
implementation_notes: C has no exception machinery, so the mute is a convention rather than a construct: an expression statement is already evaluated as a void expression, and CERT EXP12-C asks for the cast to be written explicitly - `(void)close(fd);` - to signify programmer intent when a return value is deliberately not checked. Put the documented, inconsequential condition next to it (EBADF on an already-closed read-only descriptor, ENOENT for a file that is already gone) and prefer a non-failing form where one exists (stat() before unlink(), F_GETFD before close(), read-only descriptor when no buffered data can be lost). The classic checked-and-handled form is still correct whenever the call can return a value with consequences: EIO on a write, short read/write, EINTR on a blocking call that must be retried.
pitfalls: Silently dropping a return value is indistinguishable from forgetting to check it: without the explicit (void) cast and the comment, neither -Wunused-result/[[nodiscard]] nor a reviewer can tell intent from omission.

errno is only meaningful immediately after a failing call and is not cleared by a succeeding one, so a checker must test the return value (or set errno = 0 first) - otherwise a stale errno makes an ignored failure look justified, or a real one look harmless.
EINTR and partial I/O are not ignorable by default: muting them discards retries and short-transfer handling the operation still needs, and the failure surfaces later as truncated data.
